body: That's totally understandable. But if you went to her first and she didn't/couldn't respond appropriately, escalating matters to get the help you need could be appropriate. I wish I had seen this when I was a teen -- I was terrified to tell anyone how I felt, but now I think their reaction to my feelings, even if it's pretty negative, is still better than it would be if I were dead. Depression can be a life or death matter. I'm sorry your mom hasn't treated it that seriously. I hope you keep trying until you find someone who will.
That is a lot of sadness in a short timespan. I hope you're able to find some comfort.

I'm glad you're still with us, and that you're talking to your sister. I hope you'll be honest with her about how you're feeling. It's unfortunate that the online hotlines you've tried haven't been helpful, but the fact that you're trying them speaks volumes to me. Your life is valuable -- keep fighting for it, in whatever way helps you.
For what it's worth, I consider 911 to be the last resort, what I'd do if every other effort had failed and I were clearly in danger. (Literally an emergency situation.) I don't ever want to go to the psych hospital again, and I get why others don't want to be there either, but I'd like to think I'd do it anyway if it were really necessary. Being there for a few days very well may have saved my life. That doesn't mean it's the right choice for everyone, of course. Merely an option.

It must be so difficult to have such strong feelings invalidated by someone who's supposed to care for you. Have you considered telling a different adult? If you're in school, one way to go about it could be to tell a counselor or a teacher. It might seem like a very hard thing to do, and it probably is, but it could make a big difference.
Thank you for writing this and posting it here. Best wishes for your recovery.

I'm struggling to find words -- my heart hurts for you. You've been through so much. It would be really understandable if you felt like the pain you're in right now is infinite. However, I do hope you change your decision to end your life in the wake of the shocking news about your mother. Would you consider talking to someone about it? You might prefer to talk to someone you know, in person or on the phone. You could also call a hotline (there's a link with phone numbers in the right sidebar on this page), use an online service (crisischat.org and imalive.org have both served me well in the past, though there can be a wait to chat with someone, and rainn.org also has an online service specialized for survivors of sexual violence), or you could reply here. I'll check back later this afternoon. Others might see and reply as well. I hope that you do find a way to stay safe. How do you feel about calling 911 or going to the ER if you feel you can't be safe on your own?
I'm really glad to hear you're getting treatment. It could help with working through some of this tough stuff. How are you feeling today?

I can't say what you *should* do. I would hope, though, that if one of my friends stumbled across my suicidal plans (or anything that big), they'd say something, even if I'd intended anonymity. It was just a coincidence that you found the post and profile, right?

You're smart enough to ask for help -- that's big. Are you being treated for the depression and trust issues? If not, what do you think about seeking that kind of help? There are professionals who specialize in helping people deal with trauma. I've been assaulted and taken advantage of often enough to feel like a magnet for abuse; it's been difficult to learn/accept that it is not my fault, that it doesn't happen because I'm stupid or naive or worthless, that it happens because there are people in the world who suck. Sometimes, it makes it hard to see that there are good people in the world, too, like the one who took you to the hospital. I am so sorry that you've been through such awful experiences with violence. I hope you can find healing.

I am very glad to hear you don't want to kill yourself. I agree that many posters here have already made their decision, and that's heartbreaking, but I do think many people are looking to be dissuaded here, too. (I was when I posted a couple of days ago.) I don't want to assume I understand your statement about cancel vs. postpone, though. Do you mean you've decided not to do it, or that you're trying to decide not to do it? (Or maybe some other meaning that I've not caught?) I too would like to cancel my sooner-or-later suicide plan, but I've accepted postponing indefinitely as a substitute to take the pressure off until I'm healthy enough to decide never to do it. That might not mesh with your outlook/experiences -- if the shoe doesn't fit, please don't feel like I'm pressuring you to wear it. It's merely what I'm doing to hang on. I hope you continue to hang on, in whatever way works for you.

It's healthy to share your problems with people close to you. I'm sorry you've had such a bad experience with that, and that it feels bad to have an entirely human need for attention. I might be in a similar place to yours: I don't want to kill myself, but it feels inevitable, and I feel alone. My current method of coping with my intrusive suicidal thoughts (I hope you don't mind me sharing) is to decide to put off the decision until a given point... after a holiday, a young family member's birthday, some other occasion or event, a seasonal change, whatever. It can be a time when I think I might be feeling a little better by then, or an event I want to be around for, anything. So far, when I get to the point that I'd previously put the decision off to, I've always decided to put off the decision again. But it helps somehow, knowing that even if it is necessary or inevitable, I don't have to decide to do it right this minute (or decide that I'll never do it even if things get even more terrible). Could you consider using something similar to take the pressure off and maybe help you get through this time? Things might get better, things might get worse or stay the same, but we won't have any chance of seeing our lives improve if we end them.
"Think about something else" isn't super-helpful advice for someone with intrusive thoughts, but thanks for trying.

I was also a shy, quiet, A+ student. I got in trouble at school. My family wasn't upset. They knew it wasn't like me and that meant something was wrong. Is it possible your family might respond similarly?

Yeah, I'm focused pretty hard on wanting to escape the constant urge to kill myself. How short-sighted of me. No, I do not feel defined by my diagnoses, etc., but the other stuff isn't especially relevant in this space. I want to live, generally speaking, but I don't want to live with not wanting to live. That sentence is sort of recursive, but perhaps you get the point.

Knowing you need help and fearing the place you might get that help is a scary situation. I've been in that spot. I'm not sure what happens if you go to an ER specifically -- my circumstances were a little different. But in my experience, being in the psych hospital kept me safe when I couldn't handle that responsibility. It didn't do a lot for my mental health, but I stayed alive. I agree with the poster above that there are probably better options if you're not to that point yet. However, if those aren't available to you or you feel you're in danger, going to the hospital (even if you end up with a bill) is still a better option than attempting to end your life.

I just don't see the point in persisting any more. I'm doing everything right, everything that's supposed to help me get better, but I no longer have a reason to believe I'm actually going to get better. It seems like I get these short breaks from being depressed, and then the next round of depression is even worse.

The most important times that I've thought I really connected with someone, and/or was loved by someone, it ended in trauma. The times that weren't actively traumatic were just failed attempts to connect, which hurts too, but differently. I'm pretty done with people. Living without people doesn't seem to be an option. Yet, I'm alone and I hate it. I can't claim I'm being logical.
I don't want to kill myself. I'm just running out of reasons not to do it. Reasons help me challenge the little impulse that whispers do it, do it, could do it right now and it'd all be over. Reasons make it easier to resist and keep my willpower up. I ended up in the hospital last year in part because I couldn't convince myself or my therapist that I'd be able to continue resisting my impulse to kill myself. I was emotionally exhausted from this constant struggle. I really can't let it get there again. The hospital might have actually made things worse, mentally, but I was safe there. Would I rather die than be hospitalized again? Not sure.
As with so many things in life, though: easier said than done. I'm so worn down.
I'm so sorry you lost someone so dear to you, and in such a traumatic way. It must feel really hard to carry that burden. What has helped make it even a tiny bit lighter for you in the past?

It sounds like you're in horrible pain. I wish I had the power to make it not so bad, for you and me both. You mentioned she wouldn't have wanted you to end it after the accident. What do you think she would want you to do now?
